latest_apis.rationale: App-side code is consistently on the current generation (Nuxt 4 structure, awaited useFetch, useId, reactive useHead, clearError), and the pinned majors are exactly the current stable ones. The deductions are the pre-4.6 server-import style that the brand-new nuxt/server surface was introduced to replace, and ignoring 4.6's route-typed fetch in favor of hand-written generics.

churn_resistance.rationale: Data access and configuration are genuinely well-isolated — an upstream API change touches one module — but the churn-reduction constructs the rubric names are missing where it counts: payload types are copy-pasted by hand at the boundary with no shared source of truth (Nuxt's shared/ dir and route-typed fetch exist for this), no tsconfig/type-check exists to detect drift, and server code uses the import style the framework just superseded. A framework upgrade or a payload-shape change ripples across several files silently.

findings.issue: All five server handlers (also abilities/[name].get.ts:1, moves/[name].get.ts:1, types/[name].get.ts:10, types/index.get.ts:1) rely on the auto-imported h3 defineEventHandler/getRouterParam family. Nuxt 4.6 added the nuxt/server import surface specifically so this code runs unchanged on Nuxt 5's Nitro v3/h3 v2; the blog says the auto-imported helpers are still h3's and to import from nuxt/server explicitly.
findings.suggestion: Import defineEventHandler, getRouterParam, createError from 'nuxt/server' in the server routes and utils; this is the documented forward path and removes most of the Nuxt 5 migration surface.

findings.issue: Payload interfaces are hand-duplicated per page (IndexData, PokemonData, MoveData, AbilityData, TypeData) against server routes whose returns are any-derived, with no compiler check tying them together; EvolutionNode is defined verbatim in both app/server/api/pokemon/[name].get.ts:10 and app/app/components/EvolutionList.vue:2.
findings.suggestion: Move the DTO interfaces into Nuxt's shared/ directory (or type the server route returns directly) so both sides import one definition, and enable experimental.routeTypedFetch so useFetch infers the payload types from the routes.

findings.issue: No root tsconfig.json containing the project references Nuxt 4 requires, and no devDependencies (typescript/vue-tsc), so there is no type-check step at all despite ~95 lines of hand-written interface declarations that must stay in sync by hand.
findings.suggestion: Add the documented tsconfig.json (references to ./.nuxt/tsconfig.{app,server,shared,node}.json) and a typecheck script with vue-tsc, so interface drift fails CI instead of surfacing at runtime.

findings.issue: Upstream fetches have no timeout or abort; a slow or stuck PokeAPI response will hang the SSR render indefinitely with no recovery path.
findings.suggestion: Pass a signal: AbortSignal.timeout(ms) to fetch (or use $fetch/useFetch's timeout option), and surface the abort as a 5xx error.

findings.issue: A hand-rolled in-memory promise cache with TTL and ad-hoc eviction re-implements what Nitro's defineCachedFunction (or route-rule/routeRules caching) provides for free — TTL, in-flight dedupe, and pluggable storage that could move to Redis/filesystem without code changes.
findings.suggestion: Wrap pokeapi() in defineCachedFunction({ maxAge, name, getKey }) or add routeRules caching for the hot routes (e.g. /api/pokedex); delete the bespoke Map.

findings.issue: Query strings are reconstructed with key.split('?') and template concatenation, an easy place for encoding bugs when a path ever contains a '?'.
findings.suggestion: Build the request URL with new URL(path, base) and set searchParams, which handles joining and encoding correctly.

findings.issue: Lockfile pins nuxt 4.6.2 while 4.6.3 (2026-10-27) carries security fixes, including a dot-segment request-path bypass (GHSA-9v7c-q64q-vv33); the ^4.6.2 range allows it but npm install honors the lockfile.
findings.suggestion: Refresh the lockfile to 4.6.3 as part of routine maintenance.

findings.issue: No future.compatibilityVersion: 5 preparation; the 4.6 release notes list several Nuxt 5 defaults (typed pages, route-typed fetch, navigateTo early return) that, once flipped, will change inference and behavior in this codebase untested.
findings.suggestion: Enable the future flag (or individual experimental options) once type-checking is in place, so the Nuxt 5 upgrade is a config change rather than a surprise.

findings.issue: The wrapper discards status/refresh and asserts `data as Ref<T>`, hiding the undefined-able nature of the ref and weakening the boundary type.
findings.suggestion: Type the return as Ref<T | undefined> or Narrowable<T> and surface the refresh function, so callers can't assume data without checking.

summary: A genuinely current Nuxt 4 app — right majors, right structure, current data-loading and component APIs, and a three-dependency footprint. It ages well where it matters most (all upstream access behind one module, one data-loading composable, config in one small file), but it was written on Nuxt 4.6 without adopting 4.6's own future-proofing: the nuxt/server import surface, route-typed fetch, and a shared type layer, leaving hand-duplicated boundary types with no type-check to catch drift. A Nuxt 5 upgrade or a payload change would touch several files silently.
